transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Roman.
Stephen Miller is set to take over Monday as White House Chief
of Staff replacing Susie Wiles, who resigned Friday.
Miller is the architect of many
of President Trump's more controversial domestic policies,
including immigration reform.
Now, many Democrats are saying Trump made the wrong choice
for the position.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries,
who's expected to become the next speaker
in the next Congress, was on ABCs this week.
>> It was an irresponsible decision, in my view.
There's not going to be any opportunity, certainly,
to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents.
And we're committed to forcefully pushing back
against the extremism that they may try to continue
to unleash on the American people.
And we've got a firewall in the House
and a firewall in the Senate, thanks to the American people.
>> Jeffries earlier called Miller, quote, a malignant tumor,
and the president should have fired him instead
of promoting him.
Investors on Wall Street are gearing
up for the latest inflation report.
It's due out this week.
As NPR's Rafael Naum reports, the data comes at a time
when there are fears
about artificial intelligence hitting stocks.
>> The U.S. is set to report how much consumer prices rose
in October at a time when voters have said they're struggling
with the cost of living in the most recent midterm elections.
One thing to note is that there's not going
to be a comparison to a year ago because of a government shutdown
that prevented the Labor Department
from compiling the report in October last year.
But investors will be seeing how consumer prices fared last month
compared to September to get a better gauge
of how inflation is doing.
The report comes at a time when stock markets are
under pressure amid fears about the outlook for AI shares.
Rafael Naum, NPR News.
>> Israel is taking a step toward possibly ousting its
longest-serving leader, Benjamin Netanyahu's top rival has been
tapped to form the next government.
NPR's Lauren Frayer reports Gadi Isincott is facing a number
of challenges putting together that governing coalition.
>> Gadi Isincott is a former Israeli military chief whose
soldier's son was killed in combat in Gaza.
He briefly served in Prime Minister Netanyahu's cabinet
before quitting, forming a new party and challenging him.
Neither man won a majority in last month's election,
but most other parties have said they want Isincott to govern.
He's got to build a coalition, though, first,
which could include Arab-led parties.
Palestinian citizens of Israel voted in record numbers.
It could also include ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties,
which are demanding exemption from military service.
Isincott has about six weeks to form a government during which
Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister and could try
to thwart his efforts.
Lauren Frayer, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
>> And from Washington, you're listening to NPR News.
Pope Leo has wrapped up his time in Uruguay.
It's the first country of his three-nation visit.
He'll next visit in Latin America.
He arrives later today in Argentina.
>> Aliah Hertzler McCain of Religion News Service reports.
>> Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, was Argentine,
but he never went back to his home country.
Leo will be the first pope to visit Argentina since 1987.
An official with the city of Buenos Aires
has said they expect about two million people
to attend mass at the Monomento de Los Españoles.
Leo will also visit a residential center
for people with disabilities,
where some Argentine Catholics hope he will speak
against government cutbacks to social programs.
On Wednesday, Leo will celebrate mass in Lujan,
a key pilgrimage site for devotion to Mary.
Later on Wednesday, Leo will fly to Peru,
the country where he was a missionary and a bishop.
For NPR News, I'm Aliah Hertzler McCain.
>> With Democrats in the Senate
now holding 54 seats in the next Congress,
two seats remain undecided, Alaska and Mississippi,
where the Democratic candidates hold a narrow lead.
Former Congresswoman Mary Peltola holds
about a 600-vote lead over incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan,
with an estimate a little more than 70% of the vote counted.
In Mississippi, former prosecutor Democrat Scott Colum
leads the incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde Smith
by more than 2,000 votes, with 97% of the vote tally.
Neither race has been called.
In the House, Democrats could head into the new Congress
with a more than 80-seat majority.
>> I'm Dan Roman, NPR News, Washington.
